abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine was emerging as a promising treatment for tumor immunotherapy. Highly efficient antigen-presenting ability in tumor immunotherapy through splenic dendritic cell (DC)-targeting mRNA delivery system was very important, but it remained a great challenge. In this study, a library of gemini-like ionizable lipid (termed H-type ionizable lipid, HIL) was synthesized and used for constructing mRNA-encapsulated nanoparticles (mRNA/HNPs) for in vivo mRNA delivery. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis indicated that the spleen-targeting transfection efficiencies of mRNA were strongly correlated with the apparent pKa values of mRNA/HNPs after intravenous injection. After formulation screening, the optimized mRNA/HNPs based on H18 lipid (mRNA/H18NPs) with an average particle size of 124.4 ± 2.4 nm and a multilamellar concentric nanostructure were successfully prepared. Interestingly, without any ligand modification, the mOVA/H18NPs exhibited splenic DC-targeting mRNA transfection, and markedly increased the amounts of IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells and effector memory CD8+ T cells. Furthermore, in vivo results demonstrated that mRNA/H18NPs encapsulating antigen-encoding mRNA including ovalbumin (OVA) or tyrosinase-related protein 2 (Trp2) effectively activated antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and resulted in significant antitumor efficacy in both B16-OVA or B16F10 tumor-bearing mouse models following intravenous administration. Especially, different from the mOVA/MC3-LNPs group, the mOVA/H18NPs exhibited complete inhibition of tumor progression when it used as preventative cancer vaccines in B16-OVA tumor-bearing mouse model. These findings highlighted that mRNA/H18NPs offer a promising splenic DC-targeting delivery system for mRNA vaccines.

sec.p: Keywords: mRNA delivery, Lipid nanoparticles, Spleen-targeting, Dendritic cells, Tumor immunotherapy

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: mRNA-based therapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic approach with broad potential for therapeutic applications [[1], [2], [3], [4]], particularly in immunotherapy. This innovative modality has offered a transformative and promising strategy for treating various diseases, including infectious diseases, cancer and autoimmune disorders, by enabling precise protein expression [5,6]. Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs)-based mRNA delivery systems (BNT162b2, mRNA-1273 and mRNA-1345) has been demonstrated remarkable progress in COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention [7,8]. Although these LNPs possess excellent mRNA transfection efficiency and good biocompatibility, ensuring efficiently and safely delivering mRNA to splenic tissues for improving tumor immunotherapy still remain a great challenge.

The spleen, as the predominant secondary lymphoid organ, plays a pivotal role in modulating adaptive immune responses [9]. It had been reported that targeted delivery of mRNA cargos to splenic tissues exhibited significant therapeutic potential in tumor immunotherapy [[10], [11], [12]]. For instance, the sLNPs incorporating negatively charged stearic acid into the four-component MC3-LNPs formulation were developed and used to deliver mRNA. Following intravenous administration, ovalbumin (OVA) mRNA-loaded sLNPs elicited robust immune activation and demonstrated strong anti-tumor efficacy in both EG.7-OVA lymphoma and B16F10-OVA melanoma models, mediated by spleen-selective mRNA transfection that enabled antigen-specific immune responses [10]. In addition to charge modulation strategies, the esterase-responsive quaternium lipidoid-based lipid nanoparticles (AMB-POC18 LNPs) also achieved high-efficiency mRNA transfection in splenic tissues, particularly in splenic B cells, following systemic administration [11]. This spleen-targeting mechanism resulted from the different esterase concentration between hepatic and splenic microenvironment. In vivo results revealed that AMB-POC18 LNPs demonstrated significant tumor suppression and immune protection in a B16-OVA melanoma model. Particularly, among all splenic immune cells, dendritic cells (DCs) represent a highly attractive target due to their robust capacity for antigen recognition, processing, and presentation, thereby initiating antigen-specific T-cell immune responses. As reported, the R18D NPs assembled by the bioreducible lipophilic poly (β-amino ester) have showed preferential splenic DCs transfection (accounting for over 70% transfected splenic immune cells) following intravenous administration, and achieving significant antitumor effects in murine models of melanoma and colon adenocarcinoma [13].

Gemini-like cationic lipids are a class of amphiphiles structured with dual positively charged headgroups and two hydrophobic alkyl tails, interconnected via a linker [14], which were used in the nucleic acid delivery system [15]. For instance, carbamate-bridged gemini cationic lipids have demonstrated superior plasmid DNA (pDNA) binding affinity and significantly improved transfection efficiency for pDNA compared to the mono-head counterparts [16]. In our previous study, a disulfide-bridged gemini-like cationic lipid (ssGLCL), composed of dual lysine headgroups and two oleyl alcohol tails with a bridge, exhibited great siRNA delivery efficiencies in vitro and in vivo [17]. In addition, siRNA/ssGLCL cationic nanocomplex formed special nanostructures with tightly packed multilamellar architectures, which provided improved colloidal stability and effective protection against nuclease degradation [15]. Due to the unique structure, gemini-like cationic lipids usually exhibited relatively low critical micelle concentration (CMC) and enhanced self-assembling ability, thus making them potential utilities for nucleic acid delivery. To take these advantages, the gemini-like lipids should be rationally designed and used as ionizable lipids for the construction of spleen-targeting mRNA delivery system.

Herein, a combinatorial library of gemini-like ionizable lipids (termed H-type ionizable lipids, HILs) comprising tertiary amine headgroups (ten types), oleyl hydrophobic tail and biodegradable linker (two types) was designed and used for the construction of mRNA-encapsulated nanoparticles (mRNA/HNPs) for efficient mRNA transfection following systemic administration. After screening, the optimized H18 lipid along with other helper lipids and mRNA, was mixed in the microfluidic chip, to form the mRNA/H18NP with a unique multilamellar concentric nanostructure, which exhibited excellent dilution stability and serum stability. As shown in Scheme 1, following intravenous administration, the mRNA/H18NPs exhibited specific splenic DCs transfection without modification of additional ligands. When delivering antigen-encoding mRNA, mRNA/H18NPs were examined for immune stimulation ability using bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs) and murine models. Subsequent studies further evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of mRNA/H18NPs in tumor immunotherapy, demonstrating significant antitumor activity facilitated by robust antigen-specific CD8+ T cell response in tumor-bearing mouse models.

caption.p: Schematic illustration of in vivo tumor immunotherapy enhanced by mRNA/HNPs through intravenous injection. H18 lipid, DOPE, cholesterol, DMG-PEG2000 and mRNA were mixed to form mRNA/H18NPs with the special multilamellar concentric nanostructures. Following intravenous administration, mRNA/H18NPs demonstrated preferential adsorption of complement C3 proteins to form a characteristic protein corona, resulting in specific mRNA transfection in the spleen, especially in splenic dendritic cells. When encapsulating tumor antigen-encoding mRNA, the mRNA/H18NPs achieved precise transfection of the antigen mRNA in splenic dendritic cells. This targeted delivery stimulated dendritic cell maturation and subsequent antigen presentation, initiating robust T cell priming. The activated antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes then infiltrated into tumor tissues, ultimately inducing tumor cell elimination.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: DC2.4 cells (murine bone marrow-derived dendritic cell line), 293T cells (human embryonic kidney cell line), B16-OVA cells (murine melanoma cell line) and B16F10 cells (murine melanoma cell line) were purchased from Institute of Basic Medical Science, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (Beijing, China). 293T cells, DC2.4 cells, and B16F10 cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U mL−1 of penicillin, and 100 U mL−1 of streptomycin. B16-OVA cells were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) with 10% FBS, 100 U mL−1 of penicillin, and 100 U mL−1 of streptomycin. All cells were incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 cell incubator [18].

sec.title: Extraction and culture of BMDCs
sec.p: The femur and tibias of 6-8-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were harvested and flushed by cold PBS for multiple times. The collected bone marrow suspensions were filtered through a 70 μm nylon mesh to remove debris and muscle tissues. Afterwards, the suspensions were centrifuged at 1200 rpm for 5 min and the collected cells were resuspended in RPMI medium with 10% FBS, 100 U mL−1 of penicillin, 100 U mL−1 of streptomycin, and 20 ng mL−1 GM-CSF. The obtained cells were cultured at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 cell incubator. Half of the culture medium was replaced with fresh medium every 2 days. On the 7th day of cell culture, the suspended cells were used in the experiments [19].

sec.title: Experimental animals
sec.p: BALB/c mice and C57BL/6J mice (6-8 weeks) were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. and maintained in the specific pathogen-free (SPF) grade animal room of Peking University of Health Science Center. All animal care and experiments followed the approval of Institutional Authority for Laboratory Animal Care of Peking University (No. BCJG0179).

sec.title: Preparation and characterization of mRNA/HNPs
sec.p: Preparation: The HIL, DOPE, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000 were dissolved in ethanol at indicated molar ratio of 35:16:46.5:2.5 [20]. mRNA aqueous solution was diluted in 50 mM citrate buffer with pH 4.0 (0.1 mg mL−1). Then, the resulting mRNA solution was mixed with lipid solution in a volume ratio of 1:3 (lipid/mRNA) by microfluidic mixing to form mRNA/HNPs. mRNA/HNPs were further dialyzed against PBS buffer (pH = 7.4) with a dialysis tube (Cut-off MWCO: 3500 Da) at 4 °C overnight.

mRNA/MC3-LNPs were also prepared and used as a control group in this study. Dlin-MC3-DMA, DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000 were mixed at a molar ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5 in ethanol. The other procedures remained consistent with the preparation of mRNA/HNPs.

Formulation Optimization: In the first round of formulation screening, the mRNA/H18NPs formulation was optimized using a four-factor-five-level Response Surface Methodology, designed by Design-Expert 12. Four factors included molar ratio of nitrogen number of H18 lipid to phosphorus number of mRNA molecules, molar composition of H18 lipid in total lipids (H18 content), molar composition of DOPE in total lipids (DOPE content), and molar composition of DMG-PEG2000 in total lipids (PEG content). Each factor, level, and response value of formulation screening was listed in Table S2 and Table S3. The design of second round of formulation screening was listed on Table S4.
Size, PDI and Zeta Potential: The size, polydispersity (PDI) and zeta potential of mRNA/H18NPs were measured using Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) (Malvern Zetasizer Pro, UK) at 25 °C.

GSH-responsive disassembling of NPs: The prepared mRNA/H18NPs (20 μL) was incubated with GSH solution of different concentrations (4 mM, 16 mM, and 32 mM) at 37 °C for 4 h. Afterwards, the size and PDI of treated mRNA/H18NPs were measured using DLS.
mRNA Encapsulation Efficiency: The encapsulation efficiency of mRNA/H18NPs was measured using a Quant‐iT Ribogreen assay kit (ThermoFisher, USA) according to the instruction manual.

Measurement of apparent pKa: The apparent pKa of mRNA/H18NPs was determined by TNS assay. TNS was dissolved in distilled water at a concentration of 100 μM as a stock solution. A series of buffer solutions with a pH range of 2.5 to 11 were prepared with 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM HES, 10 mM ammonium acetate, and 130 mM NaCl. mRNA/HNPs were diluted to 100 μM (total lipid concentration) with different buffer solutions and then incubated with 1 μM TNS solution for 10 min. The fluorescence intensity was determined using a microplate reader at excitation and emission wavelengths of 321 nm and 445 nm, respectively. The fluorescence intensity of mRNA/H18NPs at different pH was fitted with sigmoidal best fit analysis. The pKa value was the pH at which half-maximal fluorescence intensity was achieved [21].

sec.title: Cytotoxicity assay
sec.p: 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay was used to evaluate the cytotoxicity of mRNA/H18NPs and mRNA/MC3-LNPs on DC2.4 cells and 293T cells. DC2.4 or 293T cells were seeded onto 96-well plates (8.0 × 103 cells/per well) and incubated in a 5% CO2 incubator for 24 h. The cells were treated with mRNA/H18NPs or mRNA/MC3-LNPs of different concentrations and incubated for 24 h. Then 20 μL MTT solution (5 mg mL−1) was added into each well. After 4 h, the medium was replaced by 150 μL DMSO, and the plates were shaken for 10 min at 37 °C. The absorbance of the cells was measured on a microplate reader at a wavelength of 490 nm.

sec.title: In vivo luciferase assay
sec.p: BALB/c mice (male, 6 weeks) were administered intravenously with mLuc/H18NPs at a dose of 0.25 or 0.5 mg mRNA/kg. For bioluminescence detection, D-Luciferin (0.2 mL,15 mg mL−1 in PBS) solution was injected intraperitoneally into the mice 10 min before imaging. The mice were anesthetized by isoflurane and placed in the imaging chamber. The bioluminescence was measured using an in vivo imaging system. Afterwards, the heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney of mice were harvested and imaged. Luminescence was quantified using the Living Image software. For the in vivo C3 depletion assay, C57BL/6J mice were pre-treated with 5 μg of Cobra Venom Factor (CVF) or PBS via intraperitoneal injection. After 24 h pretreatment, the mice were intravenously injected with luciferase mRNA-loaded H18NPs. At 6 h post mLuc/H18NPs administration, in vivo bioluminescence was measured [22].

sec.title: In vitro luciferase assay
sec.p: BMDCs were seeded in a 96-well plate (1 × 104 cells per well) on the 6th day of culture. Complement C3 protein was added to the mLuc/H18NPs solution at a mass ratio of 0.25 g C3 per gram of total lipid. The mixture was then incubated for 15 min at 37 °C. BMDCs were then incubated with untreated mLuc/H18NPs or C3-coated mLuc/H18NPs (100 ng mRNA per well) for 24 h. For antibody blockade experiments, BMDCs were pre-treated with a CR3 (CD11b) blocking antibody or an isotype control (IgG) antibody (0.25 μg per 106 cells) for 1 h at 37 °C. Subsequently, the cells were incubated with complement C3-precoated mLuc/H18NPs for 24 h. The bioluminescence was detected using a microplate reader (Varioskan LUX).

sec.title: In vitro cellular uptake assay
sec.p: BMDCs were seeded in a 24-well plate (5 × 105 cells per well) on the 6th day of culture. Complement C3 protein was added to the Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs solution at a mass ratio of 0.25 g C3 per gram of total lipid. The mixture was then incubated for 15 min at 37 °C. BMDCs were then incubated with Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs or C3-precoated Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs (1 μg mRNA per well) for 6 h at 37 °C. For antibody blockade experiments, BMDCs were pre-incubated with a CR3 (CD11b) blocking antibody or an isotype control (IgG) antibody (0.25 μg per 106 cells) for 1 h at 37 °C. Subsequently, the cells were incubated with complement C3-precoated Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs for 3 h. After treatment, BMDCs were collected, washed, and resuspended in PBS. Intracellular Cy5 fluorescence intensities were quantified using flow cytometry.

For endocytic pathway study, the DC2.4 cells were pretreated with specific endocytic inhibitors (chlorpromazine (20 μg/mL), lovastatin (250 μg/mL), amiloride (0.6 mg/mL), and EIPA (100 μM)) at 37 °C for 1 h and then treated with Cy5-mRNA-loaded LNPs at 37 °C for 3 h. For the energy-dependent uptake mechanism study, DC2.4 cells were pre-cooled at 4 °C for 1 h and then treated with Cy5-mRNA-loaded LNPs at 4 °C for 3 h. After treatment, the DC2.4 cells were collected, washed, and resuspended in PBS. The fluorescence signal of Cy5 was detected by flow cytometry. The data were analyzed using FlowJo software. The cellular uptake inhibition rate (%) was calculated by the formula: Cellular uptake inhibition rate (%) = (1 - Cy5-positive cell rate treated/Cy5-positive cell rate untreated) × 100%.

sec.title: mRNA/H18NPs transfection analysis in splenic cell subsets
sec.p: For the detection of in vivo transfection of mRNA/H18NP in splenic cell subsets, mEGFP was used as the mRNA cargo. C57BL/6J mice were intravenously injected with PBS, 15 μg mEGFP in H18NPs or MC3-LNPs. After 24 h, the spleen was excised from the mice and subsequently processed through a 70 μm nylon mesh sieve to obtain a single-cell suspension. Erythrocytes were lysed in red blood cell lysis buffer, and splenic cell subsets were labeled with Fixable Viability Dye eFluor™ 780 and then blocked with CD16/32 antibody, followed by labeling with CD45, CD3, CD11c, CD19, F4/80, ly6G, CD19, NK1.1, and MHC II antibodies (Table S7).

The proportions of EGFP+/CD11c+ MHC II+ DCs, EGFP+/F4/80+ macrophages, EGFP+/F4/80-Ly6G+ Neutrophils, EGFP+/CD3−NK1.1+ NK cells, EGFP+/CD3+ T cells, and EGFP+/CD19+ B cells were detected by flow cytometry. The data were analyzed using FlowJo software (V10).

sec.title: Protein corona analysis
sec.p: mRNA/H18NPs and mRNA/MC3-LNPs were diluted in PBS buffer to achieve a final lipid concentration of 1 mg mL−1. C57BL/6J mice were sacrificed, and the whole blood was collected in heparin-contained tube, stood for 30 min, and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The clear plasma was used for protein corona analysis. Subsequently, an equal volume of mouse plasma was mixed with mRNA/H18NPs or mRNA/MC3-LNPs solution, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 15 min. The 0.7 M sucrose solution was prepared by dissolving sucrose solid in deionized water. The resultant LNP/plasma mixtures were then layered onto a 0.7 M sucrose solution of equivalent volume and centrifuged at 15,300 g for 30 min at 4 °C. The centrifuged pellets were thoroughly washed with PBS three times. Afterwards, the pellets were resuspended in SDS-PAGE sample loading buffer (2 × ). The pellets isolated from mRNA/H18NPs and mRNA/MC3-LNPs were loaded onto 10% SDS-PAGE gel, respectively. The SDS-PAGE was performed at a constant voltage of 80 V for 20 min at room temperature, stained with Coomassie Blue for 40 min, and destained with Coomassie Blue destaining solution and distilled water for 1 h, respectively. The protein bands were cut and used for mass spectrometry analysis. Orbitrap Fusion Lumos was used to identify the constituents and abundance of the protein corona [23].

sec.title: BMDC activation and antigen presentation assay
sec.p: BMDCs were seeded in a 24-well plate (5 × 105 cells per well) on the 6th day of culture. After 24 h, BMDCs were incubated with mOVA-loaded formulations (2.5 μg mOVA per well), mLuc-loaded formulations (2.5 μg mLuc per well), or OVA protein (2.5 μg per well) for 24 h at 37 °C. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 1 μg per well) was used as the positive control group. After treatment, the BMDCs were collected, washed, and resuspended in PBS. The cells were labeled with Fixable Viability Dye eFluor™ 780 and then blocked with CD16/32 antibody, followed by labeling with CD11c, CD40, CD80, CD86, SIINFEKL, and MHC-II antibodies on ice. The labeled cells were quantified by flow cytometry analysis. Gating strategy for flow cytometric analysis of BMDCs was shown in Fig. S40.
The concentrations of cytokines (IL-4, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and IL-12) secreted by BMDCs in the cell supernatant were measured using ELISA according to the manufacturer's instructions.

sec.title: Western blotting assay
sec.p: C57BL/6J mice were intravenously injected with PBS, 15 μg OVA protein, or 15 μg mOVA in H18NPs or MC3-LNPs. After 12 h, spleens were excised from the mice and lysed with 800 μL RIPA buffer (containing 1% PMSF), and centrifuged at 12000 g for 15 min. A total of 30 μg of protein was separated by electrophoresis on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel at 80 mV for 20 min, followed by 120 mV for 60 min, and then transferred to PVDF membranes at 200 mA for 60 min. Subsequently, the membranes were incubated with 5% non-fat dry milk for 2 h, and then incubated with Anti-Ovalbumin monoclonal antibody (Abcam 306591, 1:1000 dilution) overnight at 4 °C. The membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-rabbit antibodies (1:1000 dilution) at room temperature for 1 h. The expression of OVA protein was detected using Tanon 5200Multi, with β-tubulin protein regarded as an endogenous control.

sec.title: In vivo evaluation of immune activity
sec.p: On days 0 and 5, C57BL/6J mice were intravenously injected with PBS, 15 μg OVA protein, or 15 μg mOVA in H18NPs or MC3-LNPs. On day 10, the spleen was excised from the mice and subsequently processed through a 70 μm nylon mesh sieve to obtain a single-cell suspension. Erythrocytes were lysed in red blood cell lysis buffer. The splenic cells were labeled with Fixable Viability Dye eFluor™ 780 and then blocked with CD16/32 antibody, followed by labeling with CD45, CD3, CD4, CD8, CD80, CD86, CD40, H-2Kb/OVA257-264 tetramer (Tetramer), IFN-γ, CD44, and CD62L antibodies.

The proportions of CD80+CD86+ DCs, CD40+ DCs, CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, Tetramer+CD8+ T cells, and IFN-γ+CD8+ T cells in the spleen were detected by flow cytometry. The data were analyzed using FlowJo software.

sec.title: Enzyme-linked immunospot (ELISPOT) assay
sec.p: On days 0 and 5, C57BL/6J mice were intravenously injected with PBS, 15 μg OVA protein, or 15 μg mOVA in MC3-LNPs or H18NPs. On Day 10, mice from each group were sacrificed, and splenocytes were isolated. The isolated splenocytes were seeded onto the 96-well plates precoated with specific antibodies for IFN-γ (2 × 105 cells per well), and stimulated with 2 μg mL−1 OVA peptide for 24 h. After incubation, the splenocytes were lysed and washed. The spots were visualized by incubation with a biotin-conjugated anti-IFN-γ antibody following the manufacturer's instruction. The plates were scanned using AID vSpot Spectrum and analyzed by AID Elispot 8.0 Spectrum [11,19].

sec.title: In vivo anti-tumor treatment experiments
sec.p: Therapeutic tumor models: On Day 0, B16-OVA tumor cells (2.5 × 105 per mouse) were injected subcutaneously into the flank of C57BL/6J mice. On days 5 and 10, the mice were immunized with PBS, 15 μg OVA protein, 15 μg mOVA in H18NPs or MC3-LNPs via intravenous injection. On Day 15, the mice were sacrificed, and the spleens and tumor tissues of mice were harvested for flow cytometry analysis of in vivo immune responses. Furthermore, the tumors from all groups were weighed and imaged. These collected tumor tissues were further section processed and used for KI67 staining assay, TUNEL staining assay, and CD8+ immunofluorescence analysis.

For B16F10 tumor model, B16F10 tumor cells (2.5 × 105 per mouse) were injected subcutaneously into the flank of C57BL/6J mice. On days 5 and 10, the mice were immunized with PBS, 15 μg mTrp2 in MC3-LNPs, 15 μg mTrp2 in H18NPs (high dose), 10 μg mTrp2 in H18NPs (medium dose), and 5 μg mTrp2 in H18NPs (low dose) via intravenous injection. On Day 16, the mice were sacrificed, and the whole blood, spleens, and tumor tissues of mice were harvested for flow cytometry analysis of in vivo immune responses.
The tumor volume was measured every two days and calculated according to the formula tumor volume = (tumor length) × (tumor width)2 × 0.5. Mice were euthanized when the tumor burden reached 1500 mm3.

Prophylactic tumor models: The mice were immunized with PBS, 15 μg OVA protein, 15 μg mOVA in H18NPs or MC3-LNPs every 7 days via intravenous injection. After 2 weeks (day 0), B16-OVA tumor cells (2.5 × 105 per mouse) were injected subcutaneously into the flank of C57BL/6J mice. On Day 16, the mice were sacrificed, and the spleens of mice were harvested for flow cytometry analysis.
The tumor volume was measured every two day and calculated according to the formula tumor volume = (tumor length) × (tumor width)2 × 0.5. Mice were euthanized when the tumor burden reached 1500 mm3.

Pulmonary metastasis model: B16-OVA tumor cells (2.5 × 105 per mouse) were inoculated intravenously into C57BL/6J mice. On days 5 and 10, the mice were immunized with PBS, 15 μg OVA protein, 15 μg mOVA in H18NPs or MC3-LNPs via intravenous injection. On day 16, mice were sacrificed and the lungs were harvested. The lungs were fixed with Bouin's fixative solution. The metastatic nodules were imaged and counted.

sec.title: In vivo safety evaluation
sec.p: The healthy C57BL/6J mice were treated with different formulations (PBS, OVA protein, mOVA/MC3-LNPs, or mOVA/H18NPs) via intravenous injection.

For the risk of pro-inflammatory cytokine release, serum samples of mice were collected at 6 h and 24 h post-injection, and the concentrations of cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6) were measured using ELISA assays according to the manufacturer's instructions.
For the hematological and biochemical analysis, the whole blood was collected for analysis of blood routine and blood biochemical index (BC5000Vet) 24 h after the administration.

Furthermore, major organs including heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney were also collected, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, and embedded in paraffin for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The stained slides were observed using Digital pathology slide scanner (Buchi).
The body weight of B16-OVA-bearing mice was monitored every two days during the experiment period.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All experiments were performed in triplicate unless otherwise stated. The data were shown as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Formulation screening was followed by Design-Expert 12.0. In vivo luminescence was analyzed by Living image. Flow cytometry results were analyzed with FlowJo V10. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.5 software. Two-tailed Student's t-test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed when comparing two groups or more than two groups, respectively. The survival rates of the two groups were analyzed using a log-rank test. p < 0.05 was regarded as statistically significant (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001).

sec.title: Rational design, synthesis and screening of HIL
sec.p: The H-type ionizable lipid (HIL) library comprising 20 lipid molecules was designed through the integration of three structural units (Fig. 1A): (1) Biodegradable linkers: Cystine (Cy) or homocystine (Hcy) was employed as the connecting group. The formed disulfide bonds in these linkers enabled the disassembly of the nanocarriers in the intracellular reductive microenvironment. (2) Tertiary amine group head (R1): Ten types tertiary amine head groups with different structures, including linear tertiary amines (A1-A4), cyclic tertiary amines (A5-A8), and cyclic polyamines (A9-A10), were used to tune the apparent pKa and further affected the in vivo distribution behavior and transfection efficiency of the nanocarriers. (3) Hydrophobic alkyl chains: Oleyl alcohol (OA) was utilized as the hydrophobic tail chain to improve the physical stability of nanoparticles.

caption.p: Rational design and synthesis of H-type ionizable lipid (HIL). (A) Chemical structures of three modular components of HIL used in the library. (B) Representative bioluminescence images of major organs of BALB/c mice 6 h after intravenous injection of mLuc/HNPs at a mLuc dose of 0.25 mg kg−1. Quantification of the proportion of bioluminescence intensity of specific organs (e.g., liver or spleen) to the total bioluminescence intensity of overall organs (%). Organs include heart, lung, liver, spleen, and kidney.

sec.p: As shown in Fig. S1, the H-type ionizable lipids were synthesized through four-step chemical reactions, including amine protection, esterification reaction, amine deprotection, and amidation reaction. Firstly, to avoid the intramolecular interactions, the amine groups of Cy or Hcy were protected by tert-Butoxy carbonyl (Boc) groups. Then OA was reacted with Boc-Cy or Boc-Hcy to function as the hydrophobic chain of the lipid molecules, followed by the deprotection of Boc group in acidic environment. Finally, the carboxylic acid-modified head groups were reacted with amine moieties of Hcy-OA or Cy-OA to obtain the final products (Ax-Hcy-OA or Ax-Cy-OA, abbreviated as Hx). The structures and characterization of final products (H1-H20) were shown in Table S1 and Fig. S2–S21.

After successful synthesis of HILs, twenty types of mRNA/HNPs were subsequently constructed by different HILs together with helper lipids (including DOPE, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000) according to the fixed molar ratio (35: 16: 46.5: 2.5). Luciferase-encoding mRNA (mLuc) served as the model mRNA payload throughout this study. As shown in Fig. S22A–D, all twenty mLuc/HNPs exhibited an average size range of 100-300 nm, a zeta potential range of −25 mV to +20 mV, and mLuc encapsulation efficiency range of 25%-95%. Detailed analysis of the structure-activity relationship (SAR) between the structural features of HILs and the physicochemical properties (size, zeta potential, encapsulation efficiency, and apparent pKa) of the resulting mRNA/HNPs was illustrated in the Supporting Information (Fig. S22).

Notably, predominant spleen-targeting mLuc transfection was observed in most of the mLuc/HNPs (13/20, the splenic bioluminescence flux accounted for over 70% of total bioluminescence flux) (Fig. 1B and Fig. S23). Among them, five mLuc/HNPs (H8, H13, H15, H16, and H18-based mLuc/HNPs) exhibited spleen-specific transfection with a splenic transfection proportion exceeding 85%. Moreover, mLuc/HNPs based on H6, H16, H8, and H18 (HIL with A6 or A8 tertiary amine head) exhibited significantly stronger splenic transfection efficiency than other mLuc/HNPs (Fig. S22E), which suggested the cyclic ring structure-containing amine heads were beneficial for high splenic transfection efficiency of mLuc/HNPs, potentially mediated through pKa-dependent mechanisms [24,25]. Importantly, H18-HNPs exhibited the strongest splenic transfection efficiency among these four mRNA/HNPs (Fig. 1B–S22E and S23).

To further establish the quantitative correlation between splenic transfection efficiency and apparent pKa of mRNA/HNPs, the splenic bioluminescence flux of mRNA/HNPs and their corresponding apparent pKa values were fitted to the Lorentzian regression model with an R2 = 0.9174 (Fig. S22G), as described by Equation (S1).
This finding would provide guidance for the subsequent design for LNPs based on H-type ionizable lipids.

Considering that the H18-based mRNA/HNPs exhibited the strongest splenic transfection efficiency among twenty mRNA/HNPs (Fig. 1B and Fig. S22E), the mRNA/H18-HNPs were selected as the lead nanocarrier for mRNA delivery and used for further formulation screening (hereafter referred to as mRNA/H18NPs throughout subsequent sections).

sec.title: Preparation and Characterization of Optimal mRNA/H18NPs
sec.p: To further optimize the transfection potency of mRNA/H18NPs, the formulation optimization was performed using Central Composite Design-Responsive Surface Methodology (CCD-RSM). Detailed formulation screening was described in the Supporting Information (Figs. S24 and S25). After two-round formulation screening, the formulation F-B6 (N/P = 15, molar ratio of H18: DOPE: cholesterol: DMG-PEG2000 = 50: 30: 17.5: 2.5) (Table S4) was identified as the optimal formulation of mRNA/H18NPs and prepared through the microfluidic chip for subsequent study (Fig. 2A). The optimized mRNA/H18NPs showed an average size of 124.4 ± 2.4 nm (Fig. 2B) and nearly-electroneutral properties with a zeta potential of −2.0 ± 0.6 mV (Fig. 2C). The encapsulation efficiency of mRNA within these mRNA/H18NPs was determined to be 87.6% ± 0.7%. The apparent pKa of optimized mRNA/H18NPs was 6.03 detected by 2-[(4-methylphenyl) amino] naphthalene-6-sulfonic acid (TNS) assay (Fig. 2D). In addition, in vivo transfection efficiency of these mRNA/HNPs was further validated by bioluminescence imaging in BALB/c mice following intravenous injection. As shown in Fig. S26, the bioluminescence signals of mLuc/H18NPs group were predominantly localized in the spleen tissue at all observed time points. At the 6 h time point, quantitative analysis revealed that about 87.50% of the total bioluminescence signals localized in the spleen, with only 10.79% detected in liver tissues (Fig. 2F), underscoring the spleen-targeting capability of the mRNA/H18NPs formulation.

sec.p: Notably, multilamellar concentric nanostructure morphology was observed in this mRNA/H18NPs using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Fig. 2E). This structural morphology was different from the electron-dense core structures typically reported in most LNPs [19,26]. The unique structure of mRNA/H18NPs might be attributed to the special assembly mechanism between H18 lipid and mRNA molecules (Fig. 2A). We speculated that the protonation of H18 in an acidic environment (pH = 4.0), resulted in the acquisition of positive charges by its tertiary amine groups. Due to electrostatic repulsion, the positively charged groups repelled each other and formed a special conformation, thereby minimizing repulsive forces and stabilizing the structure (Fig. S27). Under these conditions, the negatively charged phosphate groups in mRNA backbone were interacted electrostatically with the positively charged headgroups of H18 molecules, facilitating the formation of the observed multilamellar concentric structure. The detailed assembly mechanism will be systematically investigated in future studies.

To investigate the storage, dilution, and serum stability of mRNA/H18NPs, the changes in size and PDI were evaluated under different conditions. As shown in Fig. 2G–I, the particle size, PDI, and in vivo splenic transfection efficiency of mLuc/H18NPs remained stable for at least 7 days when stored at 4 °C. In addition, the mRNA/H18NPs showed remarkable dilution stability with a consistent hydrodynamic diameter of approximately 150 nm, even after 512-fold dilution in PBS (Fig. 2I). Furthermore, the mRNA/H18NPs exhibited strong serum stability, as evidenced by negligible changes in particle size following 12-h incubation with 10% fetal bovine serum at 37 °C (Fig. S28). These findings collectively suggested that the mRNA/H18NPs possessed robust structural integrity even under both extreme dilution conditions and biological fluid exposure, which is essential for protecting mRNA payload from enzymatic degradation during blood circulation. The excellent stability of mRNA/H18NPs might be correlated with their unique multilamellar concentric nanostructures.

Due to the disulfide bond in the structure, H18 molecules would be cleaved at intracellular reductive microenvironment, so that mRNA/H18NPs were expected to achieve reductive responsive disassembly. To assess the reductive responsive disassembly capability of mRNA/H18NPs, the changes in hydrodynamic size of mRNA/H18NPs were evaluated following incubation with various concentrations of glutathione (GSH) (4 mM, 16 mM, or 32 mM). As the GSH concentration increased, the size of mRNA/H18NPs progressively expanded from 150 nm, to 220 nm and further to 320 nm, accompanied by an increase in the PDI from 0.1 to over 0.4 (Fig. S29A–B). Additionally, an obvious transition of particle size distribution from monodisperse to multi-disperse was observed in 4 mM GSH-treated group compared with untreated group (Fig. S29C). These results implied that mRNA/H18NPs underwent disassembly in response to intracellular reductive environments, thereby facilitating the efficient release of encapsulated mRNA cargo into the cytoplasm.

sec.title: In vivo splenic DC-specific transfection of mRNA/H18NPs
sec.p: To further characterize in vivo cell-specific transfection efficiency of mRNA/H18NPs, the expression of enhanced green fluorescence protein (EGFP) in splenic immune cell populations was analyzed using flow cytometry at 24 h following intravenous administration of mEGFP/H18NPs into mice. Surprisingly, the highest percentage of EGFP-positive cells was found in DCs (11.17%), significantly surpassing that observed in other splenic immune cells: macrophages (1.73%), NK cells (1.78%), neutrophils (1.16%), T cells (0.19%), and B cells (0.09%) (Fig. 3A). Moreover, the mEGFP/H18NPs group exhibited 1.84-fold higher EGFP-positive percentage in DCs compared to the mEGFP/MC3-LNPs group. These results demonstrated that mRNA/H18NPs can be a potent delivery system for splenic-DCs targeting transfection in vivo.

sec.p: Furthermore, the mechanism underlying the splenic DC-specific transfection mediated by mRNA/H18NPs was also investigated. It was reported that upon entering the bloodstream, nanoparticles were rapidly coated by various plasma proteins, forming a protein corona that critically influences in vivo behavior and biodistribution of nanoparticles [[27], [28], [29]]. To characterize the protein corona associated with the mRNA/H18NPs, mass spectrometry proteomics methodology was performed to analyze the composition of adsorbed plasma proteins on mRNA/H18NPs following a 15-min incubation with mouse plasma. It was identified that 891 different proteins were adsorbed to the surface of mRNA/H18NPs. Nearly 87.4% of these proteins presented at relatively low abundance (<0.1%). As shown in Fig. 3B–D and Table S5, the protein corona of mRNA/H18NPs group was mainly composed of the complement proteins (20.31%), immunoglobin (9.70%), lipoprotein (7.05%), cytoskeleton proteins (5.08%) and coagulation factors (4.57%). Importantly, proteomic analysis revealed a striking enrichment of complement proteins in the mRNA/H18NPs group, with adsorbed complement proteins accounting for 20.31% of the total corona composition, significantly higher than those in the mRNA/MC3-LNPs (13.28%) and control (7.85%) groups (Fig. 3D). Among these absorbed proteins, complement C3 protein ranked first in relative abundance (Fig. 3B), and the abundance of complement C3 in the mRNA/H18NPs was significantly higher than that in mRNA/MC3-LNPs and control groups (Fig. 3E). Furthermore, other complement proteins, including properdin (Cfp) and complement C5 (C5) protein were also significantly enriched in mRNA/H18NPs group compared to the control groups (Fig. S30A). These findings suggested that complement pathway-associated proteins, particularly complement C3 protein, were more inclined to adsorb on the surface of mRNA/H18NPs and contributed to the splenic DC-targeting transfection of these C3-absorbed nanoparticles, which is consistent with the previous studied that complement C3 might be critical for spleen-targeting liposomes [30]. Complement proteins are known to play a central role in immune response, enhancing the phagocytic capacity of DCs and macrophages to neutralize exogenous pathogens and virus [31].

Additionally, the mRNA/H18NPs group exhibited a marked reduction in the abundance of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) compared to the mRNA/MC3-LNPs group. In contrast, the mRNA/MC3-LNPs group showed a higher abundance of ApoE than that in the control group (Fig. S30B), consistent with other reports [28]. This observation was consistent with the previous report that ApoE can facilitate liver-targeting mRNA delivery by binding to low-density lipoprotein receptors (LDL-R) expressed in hepatocytes [32]. We speculated that the obvious decrease in liver-specific transfection efficiency of mRNA/H18NPs might be correlated to the lower abundance of ApoE among the protein corona of mRNA/H18NPs.

To validate the important role of complement C3 in spleen-targeting ability of mRNA/H18NPs, in vivo C3 depletion experiments were performed. C57BL/6J mice were pre-treated with Cobra Venom Factor (CVF) via intraperitoneal injection. After 24 h, the mice were intravenously injected with mLuc/H18NPs. As shown in Fig. 3F and G, compared to the PBS-pretreated group, CVF pretreatment caused a significant reduction (∼86.3%) of luciferase expression in the spleen transfected by mLuc/H18NPs, suggesting that complement C3 enriched in protein corona was vital for the specific splenic transfection of mRNA/H18NPs.

To further investigate the role of complement C3 protein in mediating the cellular uptake and transfection efficiency of mRNA/H18NPs in DCs, Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs and mLuc/H18NPs were firstly pre-coated with complement C3 protein for 15 min, and then incubated with bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs) for in vitro analysis. As shown in Fig. 3H, a significant increase in cellular internalization (1.73-fold) was found in BMDCs treated with C3-coated Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs compared to uncoated Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs. Moreover, a marked increase in transfection efficiency (1.63-fold) was also found in BMDCs treated with C3-coated mLuc/H18NPs compared to uncoated mLuc/H18NPs (Fig. 3I). These results suggested that the enrichment of complement C3 in the protein corona promoted internalization of mRNA/H18NPs in DCs.

As reported, complement C3 primarily exerted its function through interactions with its receptors (e.g., CR3, CD46) [33,34]. In which, CR3 (CD11b) was the primary receptor responsible for the recognition and uptake of C3-opsonized nanoparticles [35]. To verify the hypothesis that CR3 receptor might be a specific mediator for cellular internalization of C3-coated mRNA/H18NPs, CR3 antibody blockade experiments were further performed. As shown in Fig. 3H, the cellular uptake of C3-coated Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs was significantly reduced by approximately 39% in BMDCs pretreated with an anti-CR3 antibody. Similarly, the luciferase expression of C3-coated mLuc/H18NPs was also significantly reduced by 21% in BMDCs pretreated with an anti-CR3 blocking antibody (Fig. 3I). In contrast, either cellular uptake or luciferase expression of C3-coated mRNA/H18NPs in BMDCs, no significant change was observed between pretreated with an anti-IgG antibody and untreated. These findings suggested that complement C3 played a critical role in facilitating the cellular uptake and transfection of mRNA/H18NPs, potentially through interactions with the CR3 receptors on DCs.

Furthermore, the difference of cell uptake behavior between Cy5-mRNA/MC3-LNPs and Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs was conducted on DC2.4 cells. As shown in Fig. S31, no significant inhibition in cellular uptake of both Cy5-mRNA/MC3-LNPs and Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs was observed in chlorpromazine, amiloride, and EIPA-treated groups. However, the strongest inhibition on cellular uptake of Cy5-mRNA/MC3-LNPs was found in the lovastatin-treated group (about 82.9% inhibition). Surprisingly, the strongest inhibition on cellular uptake of Cy5-mRNA/H18NPs was found in the 4 °C-treated group (about 83.6% inhibition). These significantly different results revealed that caveolae-mediated endocytosis was the predominant pathway for the cellular uptake of mRNA/MC3-LNPs, while mRNA/H18NPs were internalized predominantly through an energy-dependent endocytic pathway in DCs. Considering that receptor-mediated cellular uptake was regarded as an energy-dependent endocytic pathway [36], we believed that the results of mRNA/H18NPs related with 4 °C condition were probably attributed to the CR3 receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway on dendritic cells.

Taken together, mRNA/H18NPs possessed the splenic DC-targeting transfection capability without the need for additional targeting ligands (e.g., antibodies or signaling molecules). The formation of a complement protein-enriched corona on mRNA/H18NPs, particularly the high abundance of adsorbed Complement C3, appears to play a crucial role in mediating enhanced uptake and transfection efficiency in splenic DC through CR3 receptor-mediated endocytosis.

sec.title: In vitro and in vivo immune responses mediated by mOVA/H18NPs
sec.p: Splenic DCs represent a crucial subset of antigen presenting cells, playing a pivotal role in bridging innate and adaptive immunity. Their specific capacity for phagocytosis, processing, and presenting antigens to T cells enables splenic DCs as central orchestrators of immune activation [37]. Leveraging the advantages of mRNA/H18NPs on mediating splenic-DCs specific transfection in vivo, a tumor vaccine platform was developed utilizing ovalbumin (OVA)-encoding mRNA (mOVA) as a model antigen for evaluation of immune activation effects in vitro and in vivo.

Generally, the majority of tissue-resident DCs exist in an immature state, characterized by limited expression of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, which are essential for antigen presentation, and lacking co-stimulatory signals (such as CD40, CD80, and CD86) required for effective T cell activation [37]. The maturation and functional activation of DCs, marked by upregulation of MHC and co-stimulatory molecules along with secretion of immunomodulatory cytokines, represent a key innate immune event that enables efficient antigen presentation and priming of antigen-specific naïve T cells [38,39]. To assess the capacity of mOVA/H18NPs to induce DC maturation in vitro, the expression levels of key maturation markers (CD80, CD86, and CD40) in BMDCs were analyzed using flow cytometry after incubating BMDCs with mOVA/H18NPs for 24 h. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a potent microbial component known to robustly induce DC maturation, served as the positive control [37,40]. As shown in Fig. 4A–D, a significant increase in the percentages of CD80+CD86+ BMDCs (1.23-fold) and CD40+ BMDCs (1.49-fold) was seen in the mOVA/H18NPs group compared to the mOVA/MC3-LNPs group, indicating the stronger stimulation ability of mOVA/H18NPs on BMDC maturation. It is noteworthy that the percentages of CD80+CD86+ and CD40+ DCs in cells treated with mLuc-loaded H18NPs (mLuc/H18NPs) were similar to those treated with mOVA/MC3-LNPs group. Furthermore, significantly increased amounts of CD80+CD86+ DCs (1.15-Fold) and CD40+ DCs (1.68-Fold) were observed in the mLuc/H18NPs group when compared to those of mLuc/MC3-LNPs group (Fig. 4C and D). This difference revealed that H18NPs components could exhibit the self-adjuvant effects on promoting BMDC maturation, which is probably related to the activation of STING pathway by azepanyl amine head of H18 lipid [19,41].

Quantification analysis for CD80+CD86+ cells (A) and CD40+ cells (C) in BMDCs. Representative flow cytometry contour plots (B) for CD80+CD86+ cells and histograms (D) for CD40+ cells in BMDCs. Concentrations of IL-4 (E), TNF-α (F), IFN-γ (G) and IL-12 (H) in BMDCs medium detected using ELISA. Data were shown as mean ± SD (n = 3).

sec.p: Mature DCs can process antigens into MHC class I- and class II-peptide complexes, which are presented to CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, respectively, to initiate antigen-specific immune responses [37]. To further verify the antigen presentation ability of mOVA/H18NPs-induced mature BMDCs, the percentages of MHC-I-restricted OVA257-264 epitope SIINFEKL-positive cells and the percentages of MHC-II-positive cells in BMDCs were quantified using flow cytometry. As shown in Fig. S32, the highest percentages of SIINFEK+ and MHC-II+ cells in BMDCs were found in the mOVA/H18NPs group among all treatment groups, suggesting that mOVA/H18NPs treatment significantly promoted antigen presentation on MHC class-I and MHC class-II of BMDCs.

In addition, mature DCs can also secret various pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., interferons (IFN) and interleukin (IL) family), which further trigger DC activation, migration, and T cell activation [38]. To evaluate the cytokine secretion profile induced by mOVA/H18NPs, the concentrations of cytokines including IL-4, TNF-α, IL-12, and IFN-γ, were measured in the culture medium using ELISA after treating BMDCs with different LNPs. As shown in Fig. 4E–H, significantly higher concentrations of IL-4 (1.85-fold), TNF-α (1.19-fold), IL-12 (2.84-fold), and IFN-γ (1.28-fold) were found in mOVA/H18NPs group than those in mOVA/MC3-LNPs group.

Collectively, as shown in these in vitro results, the increased expression of co-stimulatory signals (CD80, CD86 and CD40) and MHC molecules (MHC I and MHC II) demonstrated that mOVA/H18NPs can effectively activate the BMDCs, thereby enhancing the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-4, TNF-α, IL-12, and IFN-γ).

To further evaluate the in vivo immunostimulatory efficacy of mOVA/H18NPs, we first verified whether the nanoparticles could drive robust antigen OVA expression in the spleen. C57BL/6J mice were intravenously administered the formulations, and the expression of antigen OVA in the spleen was analyzed by Western blot at 12 h post-injection. As shown in Fig. S33, OVA protein bands could be clearly detected in the mOVA/MC3-LNPs and mOVA/H18NPs groups, while no band was observed in the PBS group. Notably, a significantly stronger expression of OVA protein was observed in the mOVA/H18NPs group than in mOVA/MC3-LNPs group, indicating the superior splenic transfection efficiency of the mOVA/H18NPs. This robust antigen expression provided the basis for further immune activation.

Subsequently, in vivo activation effects of mOVA/H18NPs on DCs and T cells were assessed. Mice were intravenously administered two doses of the formulations at Day 0 and Day 5. Splenocytes were collected on Day 10, and the expression of co-stimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86, and CD40) on DCs and the amounts of activated T cells were analyzed by flow cytometry. As shown in Fig. 5A and B, significantly elevated percentages of CD80+CD86+ DCs (2.53-fold) and CD40+ DCs (1.27-fold) were observed in mOVA/H18NPs group than those in mOVA/MC3-LNPs group, consistent with the in vitro results. These findings demonstrated that mOVA/H18NPs treatment significantly enhanced maturation of splenic DCs in vivo, likely mediated by splenic DC-targeting mOVA transfection and self-adjuvant effects of H18NPs. Moreover, the amounts of activated T cells (CD3+CD4+ T cells and CD3+CD8+ T cells) from spleen were also examined by flow cytometry. A significant increase in percentages of CD3+CD4+ T cells (1.30-fold) and CD3+CD8+ T cells (1.31-fold) in the spleen was shown in mOVA/H18NPs group compared to the mOVA/MC3-LNPs group (Fig. 5C and D). Furthermore, it was worth noting that mOVA/H18NPs treatment induced a substantial increase in the percentage of OVA-specific CD3+CD8+ T cells (16.27%) in the spleen, which was 6.9-fold higher than the mOVA/MC3-LNPs group (Fig. 5E and F). These results demonstrated that mOVA/H18NPs could significantly enhance DC maturation and T cell activation through splenic DC-targeting mOVA transfection and self-adjuvant effects.

Quantification analysis of (A) CD80+CD86+ DCs and (B) CD40+ DCs in the spleen. Quantification analysis of (C) CD3+CD4+ T cells and (D) CD3+CD8+ T cells in the spleen. Data were shown as mean ± SD (n = 3).

sec.p: It was reported that CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes can produce IFN-γ, a critical cytokine for mediating tumor-killing effects [42,43]. Given the pivotal role of IFN-γ in determining responsiveness to immunotherapy, the numbers of IFN-γ-secreting CD8+T cells in the spleen of mice were quantified by enzyme-linked immunospot (ELISpot) assay and flow cytometry after treatment with PBS, OVA protein, mOVA/MC3-LNPs, and mOVA/H18NPs. Notably, the highest percentage of IFN-γ+CD8+ T cells was detected in mOVA/H18NPs group among all treatment groups (Fig. 5G and H). The amount of IFN-γ+CD8+ T cells in the mOVA/H18NPs group was 3.06-fold higher than that in mOVA/MC3-LNPs group. As shown in Fig. 5I and J, the numbers of IFN-γ-secreting CD8+T cells induced by mOVA/H18NPs were 3-fold higher than those by mOVA/MC3-LNPs. These results indicated that mOVA/H18NPs group significantly promoted IFN-γ production by enhancing the activation of CD8+T cells, thereby potentially facilitating stronger tumor-killing effects.

Overall, as shown in vitro and in vivo results, it was demonstrated that the mRNA/H18NPs could achieve splenic DC-targeting mRNA transfection, promoting maturation of splenic DCs and enhancing antigen presentation, thereby eliciting robust antigen-specific T-cell immune responses.

sec.title: In vivo inhibition effects of mRNA/H18NPs on xenografted tumor
sec.p: Based on the in vivo splenic DC-specific transfection properties and strong immune-stimulating ability on T cells in healthy mice, the antitumor efficacy of mOVA/H18NPs as a tumor vaccine was further investigated in tumor-bearing mice. As shown in Fig. 6A, C57BL/6J mice bearing B16-OVA tumors were intravenously administered mOVA/H18NPs twice on the 5th and 10th day after tumor inoculation (0.75 mg/kg OVA mRNA). The growth of tumor volume was monitored every two days. As shown in Fig. 6B, on the 10th day after treatment, the tumor inhibition rate for mOVA/H18NPs, mOVA/MC3-LNPs, and OVA protein group were 95.9%, 74.8%, and 39.7%, respectively. It was demonstrated that the most significant tumor growth inhibition was observed in the mOVA/H18NPs group, significantly higher than that of the mOVA/MC3-LNPs group. In addition, survival analysis showed that the median survival time of mice was significantly prolonged in the mOVA/H18NPs group (>40 days) compared to those of PBS (15 days), OVA protein (17 days), and mOVA/MC3-LNPs (24 days) (Fig. 6C). Moreover, the tumor weights of all groups were also recorded on the 10th Day after treatment. The tumor weight inhibition rate of mOVA/H18NPs (95.6%) was significantly lower than that of mOVA/MC3-LNPs (72.9%) (Fig. 6D and E), which was consistent with the results of tumor volume shown above. Meanwhile, no significant differences in body weights were noted among all groups (Fig. 6F). Collectively, these results suggested that mOVA/H18NPs had significant antitumor efficacy with good biocompatibility.

sec.p: To evaluate the in vivo anti-tumor immune responses elicited by mOVA/H18NPs, the mice were sacrificed on Day 15, and the tumor tissues and spleen were excised for further analysis. The cell suspensions were prepared from tumor tissues and spleen after digestion and homogenization. CD4+, CD8+, and OVA-specific CD8+ T cells were stained with fluorescence-labeled antibody and further analyzed by flow cytometry. As shown in Fig. 6G and H, the mOVA/H18NPs group exhibited the highest percentages of CD3+CD4+ and CD3+CD8+ T cells within tumor tissues compared to all other groups. Furthermore, the tumor tissue sections were processed and used for CD8+ immunofluorescence analysis. Immunofluorescence images from tumor tissue sections revealed a markedly increase in CD8+ T cells infiltration (indicated by red fluorescence signals) in the mOVA/H18NPs group relative to OVA protein and mOVA/MC3-LNPs groups (Fig. S34), which was consistent with the flow cytometry results. Furthermore, mOVA/H18NPs group demonstrated the highest proportions of OVA-specific CD8+ T cells in both tumor tissues and spleens among all groups (Fig. 6I and J). Furthermore, immunohistochemical imaging of KI67 (a marker of cell proliferation) and TUNEL (a marker of cell apoptosis) revealed a significant reduction in in KI67 signals (brown dots) and a significant increase in TUNEL signals in the mOVA/H18NPs group compare to those of other groups (Figure S34 and Fig. 6K), indicating that mOVA/H18NPs treatment effectively suppressed tumor cells proliferation and induced tumor cell apoptosis, thereby exhibiting the most potent anti-tumor efficacy. Collectively, these results suggested that splenic DC-specific transfection of mOVA/H18NPs delivery could promote splenic DC maturation, robustly activate T cells in the spleen, and improve infiltration of activated T cells (especially OVA-specific cytotoxic T cells) into tumor tissues, ultimately resulting in suppressed proliferation and increased apoptosis of tumor cells.

Considering metastasis often occurs during the progression of solid tumors, a pulmonary metastasis mouse model was established by intravenous injection of B16-OVA tumor cells, and used to evaluate the anti-metastatic ability of mOVA/H18NPs. These mice received intravenous injections of mOVA/H18NPs on the 5th and 10th day post-tumor inoculation, respectively. After being sacrificed on the 16th day, the lungs were excised for quantitative analysis of pulmonary metastatic nodules (Fig. 6L). As shown in Fig. 6M and N, mOVA/H18NPs group exhibited the lowest number of metastatic nodules among all treatment groups, indicating the strongest anti-metastatic activity of mRNA/H18NPs. The significant anti-metastatic effect of mOVA/H18NPs against pulmonary melanoma likely involved the activation of OVA-specific CD8+ T cells in the spleen. These activated T cells subsequently trafficked to lung tissue via systemic circulation, where they led to the immune-mediated killing of tumor cells.

In addition to the B16-OVA model, tyrosinase-related protein 2-encoding mRNA (mTrp2) was selected as another tumor antigen and encapsulated in the mTrp2/H18NPs for treatment of B16F10 melanoma in mice. (Fig. 7A). mTrp2/H18NPs was tested at three different mRNA dosage: 0.25 mg kg−1 for mTrp2/H18NPs(L), 0.5 mg kg−1 for mTrp2/H18NPs(M), and 0.75 mg kg−1 for mTrp2/H18NPs(H) (Sequence of TRP2 mRNA was shown in Table S6). As a control group, mTrp2/MC3-LNPs were administered at the mRNA dosage of 0.75 mg kg−1. On the 13th day post treatment, the tumor inhibition ratios of mTrp2/H18NPs(H), mTrp2/H18NPs(M), mTrp2/H18NPs(L) and mTrp2/MC3-LNPs group were 94.6%, 82.9%, 62.3% and 47.9%. It was demonstrated that all mTrp2/H18NPs group significantly exhibited a stronger antitumor efficacy compared with mTrp2/MC3-LNPs group (Fig. 7B). Notably, despite receiving only one-third the mRNA dosage of the mTrp2/MC3-LNPs group, the mTrp2/H18NPs(L) group also demonstrated significantly superior antitumor efficacy (p < 0.05). Furthermore, survival curve analysis (Fig. 7C) showed that the tumor-bearing mice treated with mTrp2/H18NPs (H) had a survival rate of 83.3% within 40 days, which was significantly higher than that of those treated with mTrp2/MC3-LNPs. Besides, the median survival time for mice treated with mTrp2/H18NPs(M) and mTrp2/H18NPs(L) was 30d and 25d, which were also higher than those treated with mTrp2/MC3-LNPs (21d).

Quantification analysis of IFN-γ+ cells among CD3+CD8+ T cells (D) in the spleen, (E) in tumor tissues, and (F) in the blood (n = 3).

sec.p: To elucidate the potential mechanisms underlying the antitumor efficacy, the amounts of IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells in spleen, tumor, and blood of mice treated with different preparations were quantitatively evaluated by flow cytometry. In splenic tissues, it was demonstrated a dose-dependent increase of IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cell populations was observed in different groups treated with mTrp2/H18NPs(L), mTrp2/H18NPs(M), and mTrp2/H18NPs(H) groups showing 3.7%, 8.9%, and 14.6%, respectively. These values were significantly higher than those of mTrp2/MC3-LNPs group (2.7%) (Fig. 7D). Furthermore, the 2.6-fold higher infiltration of IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells was seen in the tumor treated with mTrp2/H18NPs(H) groups when compared to that of mTrp2/MC3-LNPs group (Fig. 7E), which was consistent with the tumor growth inhibition results, suggesting that mTrp2/H18NPs-induced IFN-γ+ CD8+ T infiltration in tumor tissues plays a pivotal role in antitumor responses. Additionally, the amount of IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells in peripheral blood of mTrp2/H18NPs(H) treated mice was 3.0-fold higher than that of mTrp2/MC3-LNPs group (Fig. 7F). These results indicated that mTrp2/H18NPs could significantly induce the activation of IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells through specific transfection of Trp2 mRNA in splenic DCs. These IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells were further transported into blood and infiltrated in tumor tissues, eventually exerting strong antitumor efficacy against tumor cells.

Collectively, mRNA/H18NPs encapsulating either OVA mRNA or Trp2 mRNA exhibited significant antitumor efficacy in B16-OVA or B16F10 tumor-bearing mouse models. These potent antitumor and anti-metastasis effects are likely attributed to the efficient mRNA transfection in splenic DCs mediated by mRNA/H18NPs, which could elicit a potent systemic adaptive immune response and show robust tumor killing and anti-metastasis capability.

sec.title: In vivo prevention effects of mRNA/H18NPs on tumor growth
sec.p: Although mRNA/H18NPs exhibited significant antitumor efficacy in xenografted tumor models, tumor recurrence remains predominant challenges in current cancer therapeutics. In this study, the anti-tumor efficacy of mOVA/H18NPs was further evaluated as a prophylactic vaccine in vivo. As shown in Fig. 8A, C57BL/6J mice received two-dose 7-day intervals via intravenous administrations of mOVA/H18NPs, followed by subcutaneous inoculation with B16-OVA tumor cells. Tumor volume was monitored every two days throughout the study. Notably, significant tumor suppression was achieved in the mOVA/H18NPs group, with all mice (6/6) exhibiting complete disappearance of tumors. In contrast, significant tumor progression was still observed in mOVA/MC3-LNPs group (Fig. 8B and Fig. 8D–G). Survival analysis (Fig. 8C) demonstrated that the mice treated with mOVA/H18NPs exhibited no tumor-related mortality during the 180-day observation period, achieving a survival rate (100%) which was superior to that of the mOVA/MC3-LNPs group (33.3% of mice (2/6) exhibited tumor disappearance, median survival time 75 days). No significant changes in body weight of mice were observed between the mOVA/H18NPs and PBS groups during the 21-day observation period (Fig. S35). These results demonstrated that mOVA/H18NPs could exhibit significant tumor prevention ability with good compatibility.

(B) Tumor growth curves and (C) survival rate of B16-OVA-bearing mice (n = 6). The survival rates of the two groups were analyzed using a log-rank test. sec.p: To elucidate the tumor prevention mechanisms of mOVA/H18NPs, the amount of CD8+ effector memory T cells (TEM) in the spleens of treated mice was further evaluated using flow cytometry on the 16th day after tumor inoculation. CD8+ effector T memory cells are crucial components of the adaptive immune system, playing a pivotal role in establishing long-term immunity against pathogens and tumor cells [44]. Upon re-exposure to a specific antigen, CD8+ effector memory T cells rapidly proliferate and differentiate into large numbers of CD8+ T cells, enabling efficient elimination of target cells [45]. As shown in Fig. 8H and I, the percentage of TEM (CD44+CD62L− cells) in CD8+ T cells in mOVA/H18NPs group was 1.81-fold higher than that in mOVA/MC3-LNPs group, indicating that the potent tumor-preventive effects of mOVA/H18NPs were likely associated with robust activation of CD8+ effector memory T cells. The enhanced stimulatory capacity of T effector memory (TEM) cells in the mOVA/H18NPs group demonstrated robust induction of durable antitumor immunity, highlighting its promise as a prophylactic cancer vaccine.

sec.title: Biosafety evaluation of mRNA/H18NPs
sec.p: In addition to therapeutic efficacy, the biosafety of mRNA/H18NPs was evaluated both in vitro and in vivo. The in vitro cytotoxicity of mRNA/H18NPs was assessed using MTT assay on DC2.4 and 293T cells. As shown in Fig. S36, cell viabilities of mRNA/H18NPs group exceeding 85% were seen on both DC2.4 and 293T cells at the mRNA concentration of 0.3125-2.5 μg mL−1, suggesting good biocompatibility of mRNA/H18NPs under these conditions.

To evaluate the potential risk of pro-inflammatory cytokine release triggered by mOVA/H18NPs in vivo, concentrations of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 were measured in the serum of healthy C57BL/6J mice at different time points following intravenous administration of formulations. As shown in Fig. S37, all treatment groups (OVA protein, mOVA/MC3-LNPs, and mOVA/H18NPs) induced a significant increase in serum levels of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α at the 6-h time point compared to the PBS group. Notably, the levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 in the mOVA/H18NPs group were markedly lower than those in the mOVA/MC3-LNPs group, indicating that the mOVA/H18NPs treatment elicited a significantly weaker acute inflammatory response. This was likely associated with the biodegradability and biocompatibility of mOVA/H18NPs. At the 24 h time point, the levels of these pro-inflammatory cytokines in all treatment groups had returned to baseline, showing no significant difference compared to the PBS group. These results showed the transient and reversible release of pro-inflammatory cytokines was triggered by mOVA/H18NPs, suggesting that mOVA/H18NPs might have a better biosafety profile.

To comprehensively assess potential toxicity, the hematological analysis and H&E staining assay of major organs were also carried out at the 24 h time point following administration. No significant differences were observed between PBS and mOVA/H18NPs groups in key hematological parameters (e.g., the concentrations of white blood cells (WBC), red blood cells (RBC), and hemoglobin (HGB)) or biochemical markers (e.g., ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase), AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase), and TP (Total Protein)) (Fig. S38). These results suggested that mRNA/H18NPs treatment did not induce significant abnormalities in hematopoietic, hepatic, and renal functions of mice. Moreover, H&E staining images of major organs (including heart, lung, liver, spleen, and kidney) revealed no significant tissue necrosis or pathological changes in the mOVA/H18NPs group (Fig. S39), with findings comparable to those of the PBS, OVA protein, and mOVA/MC3-LNPs groups. Taken together, these data demonstrated that mRNA/H18NPs exhibited good biosafety and potential clinical application in enhancing tumor immunotherapy.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, a library of H-type ionizable lipid (HIL) was synthesized and used to develop lipid nanoparticles (mRNA/HNPs) for in vivo mRNA delivery. It was demonstrated that a strong spleen-specific mRNA transfection was closely correlated to the apparent pKa values of mRNA/HNPs and the complement C3-based protein corona. Without any ligand modification, the optimized mOVA/H18NPs exhibited splenic DC-targeting mRNA transfection, and markedly increased the amounts of IFN-γ+ CD8+ T cells and effector memory CD8+ T cells. In vivo results revealed that antigen-encoding mRNA-loaded H18NPs could exhibit significant tumor suppression and prevention effects on B16-OVA and B16F10 tumor-bearing mouse models based on the robust antigen-specific CD8+ T cell response, mediated by the efficient splenic DCs specific mRNA transfection. Therefore, these splenic DC-targeting LNPs based on H-type ionizable lipids would be a promising and potential platform for mRNA-based tumor immunotherapy.
